claim: The diversity of proteins in nature arose from only a few thousand domain prototypes.
source: The seemingly limitless diversity of proteins in nature arose from only a few thousand domain prototypes, but the origin of these themselves has remained unclear.
evidence: This is a statement made in the abstract without specific data or citations provided in this sentence.

claim: Contemporary domains may contain vestiges of ancestral peptides that were active as co-factors in RNA-dependent replication and catalysis.
source: We are pursuing the hypothesis that they arose by fusion and accretion from an ancestral set of peptides active as co-factors in RNA-dependent replication and catalysis. Should this be true, contemporary domains may still contain vestiges of such peptides, which could be reconstructed by a comparative approach in the same way in which ancient vocabularies have been reconstructed by the comparative study of modern languages.
evidence: This is presented as a hypothesis being tested in the study.

claim: 40 fragments were identified whose similarity is indicative of common descent, yet which occur in domains currently not thought to be homologous.
source: To test this, we compared domains representative of known folds and identified 40 fragments whose similarity is indicative of common descent, yet which occur in domains currently not thought to be homologous.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on computational analysis.

claim: The identified fragments are widespread in the most ancient folds.
source: These fragments are widespread in the most ancient folds and enriched for iron-sulfur- and nucleic acid-binding.
evidence: This is supported by data presented in Table 1 showing occurrence in ancient folds.

claim: The identified fragments are enriched for iron-sulfur-binding.
source: These fragments are widespread in the most ancient folds and enriched for iron-sulfur- and nucleic acid-binding.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3 and Table 1 showing metal-binding fragments.

claim: The identified fragments are enriched for nucleic acid-binding.
source: These fragments are widespread in the most ancient folds and enriched for iron-sulfur- and nucleic acid-binding.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3 and Table 1 showing nucleic acid-binding fragments.

claim: The identified fragments represent the observable remnants of a primordial RNA-peptide world.
source: We propose that they represent the observable remnants of a primordial RNA-peptide world.
evidence: This is the main interpretive conclusion of the study based on the data collected.

claim: The origin of most present-day proteins can be attributed to combinatorial shuffling and differentiation events involving a basic set of domain prototypes.
source: The origin of most present-day proteins can be attributed to combinatorial shuffling and differentiation events involving a basic set of domain prototypes, which act as the unit of protein evolution (Anantharaman et al., 2001; Apic et al., 2001; Ponting and Russell, 2002; Orengo and Thornton, 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Domains act as the unit of protein evolution.
source: The origin of most present-day proteins can be attributed to combinatorial shuffling and differentiation events involving a basic set of domain prototypes, which act as the unit of protein evolution (Anantharaman et al., 2001; Apic et al., 2001; Ponting and Russell, 2002; Orengo and Thornton, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature.

claim: Many domains can be traced back to the time of the Last Universal Common Ancestor (LUCA).
source: Many of these domains can be traced back to the time of the Last Universal Common Ancestor (LUCA) (Kyrpides et al., 1999; Koonin, 2003; Ranea et al., 2006), a hypothetical primordial organism from which all life on earth is thought to have descended approximately 3.5 billion years ago (Glansdorff et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: LUCA is a hypothetical primordial organism from which all life on earth is thought to have descended approximately 3.5 billion years ago.
source: Many of these domains can be traced back to the time of the Last Universal Common Ancestor (LUCA) (Kyrpides et al., 1999; Koonin, 2003; Ranea et al., 2006), a hypothetical primordial organism from which all life on earth is thought to have descended approximately 3.5 billion years ago (Glansdorff et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: The origin of domains themselves is poorly understood.
source: The origin of domains themselves, however, is poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: An origin de novo by random concatenation of amino acids appears impossible due to the high sequence complexity and low folding yield of polypeptides.
source: An origin de novo, by random concatenation of amino acids, appears impossible due to the high sequence complexity and low folding yield of polypeptides, as well as to the absence of abiotic processes that could produce peptide chains of more than 5–10 residues.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about protein folding and chemistry.

claim: Abiotic processes cannot produce peptide chains of more than 5–10 residues.
source: An origin de novo, by random concatenation of amino acids, appears impossible due to the high sequence complexity and low folding yield of polypeptides, as well as to the absence of abiotic processes that could produce peptide chains of more than 5–10 residues.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about prebiotic chemistry.

claim: Local sequence and structure similarity has been identified within domains of different fold.
source: Many lines of evidence, including the identification of local sequence and structure similarity within domains of different fold (Brennan and Matthews, 1989; Doherty et al., 1996; Copley et al., 2001; Grishin, 2001b; Friedberg and Godzik, 2005; Alva et al., 2007; Andreeva et al., 2007), or the frequent construction of domains by repetition of subdomain-sized fragments (McLachlan, 1987; Andrade et al., 2001; Hocker et al., 2002; Chaudhuri et al., 2008; Remmert et al., 2010), show that domains might not constitute the only evolutionary unit of protein structure.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Domains are frequently constructed by repetition of subdomain-sized fragments.
source: Many lines of evidence, including the identification of local sequence and structure similarity within domains of different fold (Brennan and Matthews, 1989; Doherty et al., 1996; Copley et al., 2001; Grishin, 2001b; Friedberg and Godzik, 2005; Alva et al., 2007; Andreeva et al., 2007), or the frequent construction of domains by repetition of subdomain-sized fragments (McLachlan, 1987; Andrade et al., 2001; Hocker et al., 2002; Chaudhuri et al., 2008; Remmert et al., 2010), show that domains might not constitute the only evolutionary unit of protein structure.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Domains might not constitute the only evolutionary unit of protein structure.
source: Many lines of evidence, including the identification of local sequence and structure similarity within domains of different fold (Brennan and Matthews, 1989; Doherty et al., 1996; Copley et al., 2001; Grishin, 2001b; Friedberg and Godzik, 2005; Alva et al., 2007; Andreeva et al., 2007), or the frequent construction of domains by repetition of subdomain-sized fragments (McLachlan, 1987; Andrade et al., 2001; Hocker et al., 2002; Chaudhuri et al., 2008; Remmert et al., 2010), show that domains might not constitute the only evolutionary unit of protein structure.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from cited evidence.

claim: The first folded domains arose by repetition, fusion, recombination, and accretion from an ancestral set of peptides.
source: These observations led to the proposal that the first folded domains arose by repetition, fusion, recombination, and accretion from an ancestral set of peptides (Fetrow and Godzik, 1998; Lupas et al., 2001; Soding and Lupas, 2003) that emerged in the RNA world (Gilbert, 1986), in which RNA served both as carrier of genetic information and catalyst of metabolic reactions (Jeffares et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a proposal supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The ancestral set of peptides emerged in the RNA world.
source: These observations led to the proposal that the first folded domains arose by repetition, fusion, recombination, and accretion from an ancestral set of peptides (Fetrow and Godzik, 1998; Lupas et al., 2001; Soding and Lupas, 2003) that emerged in the RNA world (Gilbert, 1986), in which RNA served both as carrier of genetic information and catalyst of metabolic reactions (Jeffares et al., 1998).
evidence: This is a proposal supported by citations.

claim: In the RNA world, RNA served both as carrier of genetic information and catalyst of metabolic reactions.
source: These observations led to the proposal that the first folded domains arose by repetition, fusion, recombination, and accretion from an ancestral set of peptides (Fetrow and Godzik, 1998; Lupas et al., 2001; Soding and Lupas, 2003) that emerged in the RNA world (Gilbert, 1986), in which RNA served both as carrier of genetic information and catalyst of metabolic reactions (Jeffares et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established RNA world theory.

claim: The local similarities found in modern proteins represent the observable remnants of ancestral peptides.
source: According to this model, the local similarities found in modern proteins represent the observable remnants of such peptides.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of the model being tested.

claim: The RNA world is widely thought to have been an important intermediate stage in the origin of cellular life.
source: In the RNA world, which is widely thought to have been an important intermediate stage in the origin of cellular life, simple peptides may have been recruited by RNA to expand its functional repertoire.
evidence: This represents established scientific consensus.

claim: Simple peptides may have been recruited by RNA to expand its functional repertoire in the RNA world.
source: In the RNA world, which is widely thought to have been an important intermediate stage in the origin of cellular life, simple peptides may have been recruited by RNA to expand its functional repertoire.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the RNA world.

claim: The catalytic range of RNA molecules is restricted.
source: The catalytic range of RNA molecules is restricted (Joyce, 2002) and peptides are good chelators of metals and small molecules.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Peptides are good chelators of metals and small molecules.
source: The catalytic range of RNA molecules is restricted (Joyce, 2002) and peptides are good chelators of metals and small molecules.
evidence: This is based on established chemical knowledge.

claim: Peptides are beneficial for RNA thermostability and folding specificity.
source: Peptides are also beneficial for RNA thermostability and folding specificity, and for the formation of oligomeric complexes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about RNA-peptide interactions.

claim: Peptides are beneficial for the formation of oligomeric complexes.
source: Peptides are also beneficial for RNA thermostability and folding specificity, and for the formation of oligomeric complexes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge.

claim: Many peptides formed of the 20 proteinogenic amino acids have an intrinsic affinity for RNA and form secondary structures upon binding.
source: It is known that many peptides formed of the 20 proteinogenic amino acids have an intrinsic affinity for RNA and form secondary structures upon binding (Patel, 1999; Das and Frankel, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Protein folding would have been an emergent property of peptide-RNA coevolution.
source: In this theory, protein folding would have been an emergent property of peptide-RNA coevolution.
evidence: This is a theoretical statement about the proposed model.

claim: The comparative studies of languages and of proteins exhibit many parallels because of their shared linear nature of information storage, the high conservation of evolutionary modules, and the similarity of evolutionary constraints acting upon them.
source: The comparative studies of languages and of proteins, in fact, exhibit many parallels because of their shared linear nature of information storage, the high conservation of evolutionary modules, and the similarity of evolutionary constraints acting upon them (Gray and Atkinson, 2003; Pagel et al., 2007; Searls, 2013; List et al., 2014) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Hundreds of words in European languages contain the conserved Semitic root qnw (*qanaw-) meaning 'reed'.
source: Today, for instance, it is known that hundreds of words in European languages contain the conserved Semitic root qnw (*qanaw-) meaning 'reed' (Huehnergard, 2011), despite it having diversified into a wide range of functional forms by the same processes as already familiar from biological evolution (e.g., orthology, paralogy, horizontal transfer).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The Semitic root qnw has diversified into a wide range of functional forms by the same processes as already familiar from biological evolution (e.g., orthology, paralogy, horizontal transfer).
source: Today, for instance, it is known that hundreds of words in European languages contain the conserved Semitic root qnw (*qanaw-) meaning 'reed' (Huehnergard, 2011), despite it having diversified into a wide range of functional forms by the same processes as already familiar from biological evolution (e.g., orthology, paralogy, horizontal transfer).
evidence: This is supported by citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: The primordial β-hammerhead motif is seen in four different folds.
source: The primordial β-hammerhead motif (shown in red) is seen in four different folds, which cover a wide array of functions.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: RNA binding is the orthologous function of the β-hammerhead peptide.
source: Following our hypothesis of an origin in the RNA world, we propose that RNA binding is the orthologous function of this peptide, seen today in ribosomal protein L27 and exosome subunit RRP4.
evidence: This is a proposal based on the hypothesis and data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Protein structures diverge much more slowly than their sequences.
source: As protein structures diverge much more slowly than their sequences, structural similarity is often used for identifying such distant events.
evidence: This is established knowledge in protein evolution.

claim: Similar structures may have arisen convergently, owing to the limited number of conformations available to a folded polypeptide chain, particularly at the supersecondary structure level.
source: However, similar structures may have arisen convergently, owing to the limited number of conformations available to a folded polypeptide chain, particularly at the supersecondary structure level (Salem et al., 1999; Kim et al., 2009; Fernandez-Fuentes et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Structure similarity alone does not provide conclusive evidence of common ancestry.
source: Consequently, structure similarity alone does not provide conclusive evidence of common ancestry.
evidence: This is an inference from the previous statement about convergent evolution.

claim: The combinatorial sequence space is enormous and many sequences are compatible with a particular local structure.
source: In contrast, the combinatorial sequence space is enormous and many sequences are compatible with a particular local structure, so that sequence convergence is rare.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about sequence space.

claim: Sequence convergence is rare.
source: In contrast, the combinatorial sequence space is enormous and many sequences are compatible with a particular local structure, so that sequence convergence is rare.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about sequence evolution.

claim: Sequence similarity is a more reliable marker for common ancestry than structure similarity.
source: Thus sequence similarity is a more reliable marker for common ancestry (Soding, 2005; Kim et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The SCOPe database was used as a reference database for the assignment of domains to fold types.
source: To implement this comparative approach between domains of different fold, we needed a reference database for the assignment of domains to fold types. For this we used the SCOPe (Murzin et al., 1995; Fox et al., 2014) database (release 2.03), which is a point of reference in the classification of protein folds.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: In the SCOPe database, the first two classification levels (family and superfamily) capture homologous relationships.
source: In this database, the first two classification levels (family and superfamily) capture homologous relationships, while the grouping of structurally similar superfamilies into the same fold reflects convergent evolution, i.e. analogy.
evidence: This describes the classification system of SCOPe.

claim: The grouping of structurally similar superfamilies into the same fold in SCOPe reflects convergent evolution.
source: In this database, the first two classification levels (family and superfamily) capture homologous relationships, while the grouping of structurally similar superfamilies into the same fold reflects convergent evolution, i.e. analogy.
evidence: This describes the classification system of SCOPe.

claim: SCOPe was filtered to a maximum of 30% sequence identity (SCOPe30).
source: In order to reduce the very large background of obvious homologous matches, we filtered SCOPe to a maximum of 30% sequence identity (SCOPe30).
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: At 30% sequence identity, many relationships considered homologous by SCOPe are removed, whereas representatives for all families and superfamilies are still retained.
source: At this level, many relationships considered homologous by SCOPe are removed, whereas representatives for all families and superfamilies are still retained.
evidence: This describes the effect of the filtering procedure.

claim: The score distributions obtained were bimodal, with a higher incidence of scores at both the top, right and bottom, left of the plots.
source: In fact, the distributions we obtained were bimodal, with a higher incidence of scores at both the top, right and bottom, left of the plots.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2.

claim: The presence of some high-scoring relationships in the analogous set suggested the presence of hitherto unrecognized homologous relationships.
source: The presence of some low-scoring relationships in the homologous set (Figure 2A) did not appear too surprising, given the considerable evolutionary distance of some relationships captured in SCOPe, but the presence of some high-scoring relationships in the analogous set (Figure 2B) did, as it suggested the presence of hitherto unrecognized homologous relationships.
evidence: This is an inference from the data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: At HHsearch probabilities of 70% and TM-scores of 0.5, about a fourth of presumed homologous relationships in SCOPe30 are omitted.
source: At these threshold values, about a fourth of presumed homologous relationships in SCOPe30 and >99.95% of matches between folds, which are presumed to be analogous, are omitted.
evidence: This describes the effect of the cutoff values used.

claim: At HHsearch probabilities of 70% and TM-scores of 0.5, >99.95% of matches between folds, which are presumed to be analogous, are omitted.
source: At these threshold values, about a fourth of presumed homologous relationships in SCOPe30 and >99.95% of matches between folds, which are presumed to be analogous, are omitted.
evidence: This describes the effect of the cutoff values used.

claim: 65 clusters were obtained after automatic clustering and inspection.
source: We obtained 65 clusters, of which 20 relied on a global similarity of the folds and were omitted from further consideration.
evidence: This describes the results of the clustering procedure.

claim: 20 clusters relied on a global similarity of the folds and were omitted from further consideration.
source: We obtained 65 clusters, of which 20 relied on a global similarity of the folds and were omitted from further consideration.
evidence: This describes the filtering of the clusters.

claim: A further 5 groups were due to artifacts in domain boundaries assigned by SCOPe and were omitted.
source: A further 5 groups were due to artifacts in domain boundaries assigned by SCOPe and were also omitted.
evidence: This describes the filtering of the clusters.

claim: A final set of 40 clusters was obtained after filtering.
source: This yielded a final set of 40 clusters, within which all fragments were inspected individually, superimposed, and trimmed to a consensus length where appropriate (Figure 3, Figure 3—source data 1; Table 1).
evidence: This describes the final result of the analysis.

claim: The median length of the 40 consensus fragments is 24 residues.
source: The median length of the 40 consensus fragments is 24 residues, with the shortest fragment comprising 9 and the longest 38 residues.
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the fragment lengths.

claim: The shortest fragment comprises 9 residues.
source: The median length of the 40 consensus fragments is 24 residues, with the shortest fragment comprising 9 and the longest 38 residues.
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the fragment lengths.

claim: The longest fragment comprises 38 residues.
source: The median length of the 40 consensus fragments is 24 residues, with the shortest fragment comprising 9 and the longest 38 residues.
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the fragment lengths.

claim: The fragment lengths are in accord with the expectation that ancient peptides were simple and subdomain-sized.
source: This is in accord with the expectation that ancient peptides were simple and subdomain-sized.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data in the context of the hypothesis.

claim: Only about half of the fragments correspond to typical supersecondary structure elements.
source: Of these fragments, only about half correspond to typical supersecondary structure elements, such as α-hairpins, β-hairpins, β-meanders, and βαβ-elements (Salem et al., 1999), whereas the others are unusual fragments with odd shapes, which frequently do not form compact structures.
evidence: This is a characterization of the fragments based on structural analysis.

claim: About half of the fragments are unusual fragments with odd shapes, which frequently do not form compact structures.
source: Of these fragments, only about half correspond to typical supersecondary structure elements, such as α-hairpins, β-hairpins, β-meanders, and βαβ-elements (Salem et al., 1999), whereas the others are unusual fragments with odd shapes, which frequently do not form compact structures.
evidence: This is a characterization of the fragments based on structural analysis.

claim: The open structures of the unusual fragments reflect the association with an RNA scaffold, as still seen in ribosomal proteins today.
source: This supports the notion that they predate the emergence of hydrophobic contacts as a driving force for protein folding and that their open structures reflect the association with an RNA scaffold, as still seen in ribosomal proteins today (Soding and Lupas, 2003).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citation and comparison to ribosomal proteins.

claim: The unusual fragments predate the emergence of hydrophobic contacts as a driving force for protein folding.
source: This supports the notion that they predate the emergence of hydrophobic contacts as a driving force for protein folding and that their open structures reflect the association with an RNA scaffold, as still seen in ribosomal proteins today (Soding and Lupas, 2003).
evidence: This is an inference from the structural characteristics of the fragments.

claim: 36 of the 40 fragments had at least one match to another superfamily with a TM-score ≥ 0.5, but undetectable sequence similarity (HHsearch probability <10%).
source: To evaluate whether the sequence similarity exhibited by these fragments could be the result of biophysical constraints, rather than common descent, we searched SCOPe30 with each fragment for structurally similar matches: 36 of the 40 had at least one match to another superfamily with a TM-score ≥ 0.5, but undetectable sequence similarity (HHsearch probability <10%).
evidence: This is a result from the structural search analysis.

claim: Of the 36 fragments with structural matches, 34 had more than half of their structure matches to fragments with undetectable sequence similarity.
source: Indeed, of these 36 fragments, 34 had more than half of their structure matches to fragments with undetectable sequence similarity.
evidence: This is a result from the structural search analysis.

claim: Essentially every one of the structures detected can be formed by fundamentally different sequences.
source: This shows that essentially every one of the structures we detected can be formed by fundamentally different sequences.
evidence: This is an inference from the data on structural matches with different sequences.

claim: For the fragment set, the presumed homologous matches show a strong correlation between sequence and structure similarity.
source: For both fragment sets, the presumed homologous matches show a strong correlation between sequence and structure similarity.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5.

claim: The correlation between sequence and structure similarity in the presumed analogous matches is very weak for both the fragment set and the Smotifs.
source: In contrast, the correlation between sequence and structure similarity in the presumed analogous matches is very weak for both our fragments and the Smotifs.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5.

claim: Structurally induced sequence convergence is very low and the fragments can be formed by a broad range of different sequences.
source: This shows that structurally induced sequence convergence is very low and the fragments can be formed by a broad range of different sequences.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Biophysical constraints cannot explain the sequence similarity exhibited by the fragments.
source: Biophysical constraints can therefore not explain the sequence similarity exhibited by our fragments.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the correlation analysis.

claim: 40% (16) of the fragments have been described individually before and connected to deep evolutionary events.
source: Given the depth of analysis in many structural studies, we therefore surmised that at least some of our fragments should have been noted previously. In fact, 40% (16) have been described individually before and connected to deep evolutionary events (Figure 3, indicated by a dot; Table 1), showing that we are moving within the boundaries of established sequence-structure analyses.
evidence: This is a comparison with prior literature.

claim: The fragments comprise all but one previously reported case.
source: To our knowledge, our fragments comprise all but one previously reported case.
evidence: This is a comparison with prior literature.

claim: The ASP-box was not detected owing to the stringency of the search criteria.
source: We failed to detect the ASP-box (Figure 3—figure supplement 1: B1), found in six different folds (Copley et al., 2001), owing to the stringency of our search criteria (if the HHsearch probability cut-off is lowered to 60%, this fragment is included, along with four others).
evidence: This explains why a known fragment was not included in the main set.

claim: About a third of the fragments make contact with nucleic acids (13), based on evidence from known structures.
source: Indeed, we find that about a third of our fragments make contact with nucleic acids (13), based on evidence from known structures (fragments with a yellow background in Figure 3; Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: The Smotifs reference set yielded only 2 nucleic-acid binders, even though it covers about three times as many superfamilies and folds as the fragment set.
source: For comparison, the Smotifs reference set yielded only 2 nucleic-acid binders, even though it covers about three times as many superfamilies and folds as our fragment set (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a comparison with the reference set.

claim: The nucleic acid-binding fragments include four of the six most highly represented fragments in the dataset.
source: Our nucleic acid-binding fragments include four of the six most highly represented fragments in our dataset, particularly the helix-turn-helix motif (Sauer et al., 1982; Pabo and Sauer, 1984; Brennan and Matthews, 1989; Suzuki and Brenner, 1995; Aravind et al., 2005) (Figure 3: 1- found in 14 folds and 20 superfamilies, abbreviated in the following as 14, 20) and the helix-hairpin-helix motif (Figure 3: 2- 8, 15; Figure 4).
evidence: This is based on the data in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: Ribosomal proteins contain 8 of the 13 nucleic acid-binding fragments.
source: A special case of nucleic-acid interaction is provided by ribosomal proteins, which contain 8 of our 13 nucleic acid-binding fragments (indicated by red font color in Figure 3; Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: Ribosomal proteins are likely to represent the oldest proteins observable today.
source: Ribosomal proteins are likely to represent the oldest proteins observable today and, for the most part, still require the RNA scaffold to become structured, providing a window into the time when protein domains were being established (Hsiao et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Ribosomal proteins, for the most part, still require the RNA scaffold to become structured.
source: Ribosomal proteins are likely to represent the oldest proteins observable today and, for the most part, still require the RNA scaffold to become structured, providing a window into the time when protein domains were being established (Hsiao et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation.

claim: Of the nine folds proposed to be the most ancient, six encompass at least one of the 40 fragments.
source: For comparison, of the nine folds proposed to be the most ancient (Caetano-Anolles et al., 2007), based on the comparative analysis of proteomes from diverse branches of life, six encompass at least one of our 40 fragments (Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Table 1 and compared with cited work.

claim: Seven of the fragments coordinate metal ions and iron-sulfur clusters.
source: Seven of our fragments coordinate metal ions and iron-sulfur clusters (red background in Figure 3; Table 1), e.g., the cytochrome-heme-attachment motif (Figure 3: 17) (Mathews et al., 1985) and the 4Fe-4S coordinating peptide (Figure 3: 18) (Lupas et al., 2001), and five bind nucleotides and nucleotide-derived cofactors (blue background in Figure 3; Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: Five fragments bind nucleotides and nucleotide-derived cofactors.
source: Seven of our fragments coordinate metal ions and iron-sulfur clusters (red background in Figure 3; Table 1), e.g., the cytochrome-heme-attachment motif (Figure 3: 17) (Mathews et al., 1985) and the 4Fe-4S coordinating peptide (Figure 3: 18) (Lupas et al., 2001), and five bind nucleotides and nucleotide-derived cofactors (blue background in Figure 3; Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: In the fragments, the contribution of the peptides is the coordination of catalytic cofactors and not the provision of catalytic residues per se.
source: We note that in all these fragments, the contribution of the peptides is the coordination of catalytic cofactors and not the provision of catalytic residues per se, in accordance with a primordial role as cofactors of RNA-driven catalysis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the functional characteristics of the fragments.

claim: No domain was found that contained two or more different fragments from the set.
source: However, we did not find even one domain that contained two or more different fragments from our set.
evidence: This is a negative result from the analysis.

claim: The fragments either form their folds by repetition or in single copy, decorated by heterologous structural elements.
source: Our fragments either form their folds by repetition or in single copy, decorated by heterologous structural elements.
evidence: This is a characterization of how the fragments occur in folds.

claim: Many of the fragments might represent dominant cores that guide the folding of the remainder of the polypeptide chain.
source: At present, we find the reasons for the lack of fragment combinations unclear, but we note that many of our fragments might represent dominant cores that guide the folding of the remainder of the polypeptide chain (Religa et al., 2007) and would, as such, not be generally compatible with each other.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation.

claim: If the sequence similarity requirement is removed entirely for the 'non-significant' fragments, asking only for structural similarity (TM-score ≥ 0.5), over 50% of the families showed fragment combinations.
source: If we however removed the sequence similarity requirement entirely for the 'non-significant' fragments, asking only for structural similarity (TM-score ≥ 0.5), over 50% of the families showed fragment combinations.
evidence: This is a result from the relaxed analysis.

claim: Repetition is wide-spread, seen for 14 of the 40 fragments (35%).
source: While we were unable to detect fragment combinations, repetition is wide-spread, seen for 14 of our 40 fragments (35%) (indicated by a dotted box in Figure 3; Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: Nine of the repetitive fragments are also capable of forming folds in single copy, with additional decoration.
source: Nine of these are also capable of forming folds in single copy, with additional decoration.
evidence: This is based on the data in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: The TPR element is found in multiple copies in domains belonging to the TPR-like superfamily (a.118.8).
source: For example, the TPR element (Figure 3: 28) is found in multiple copies in domains belonging to the TPR-like superfamily (a.118.8) (D'Andrea and Regan, 2003), but only in single copy in other folds that contain it (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A and supported by citation.

claim: The TPR element occurs only in single copy in other folds that contain it.
source: For example, the TPR element (Figure 3: 28) is found in multiple copies in domains belonging to the TPR-like superfamily (a.118.8) (D'Andrea and Regan, 2003), but only in single copy in other folds that contain it (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The β-hammerhead motif is duplicated in the barrel-sandwich hybrid fold (b.84).
source: Also, the β-hammerhead motif (Figure 1B, Figure 3: 12), which resembles a hammerhead, is duplicated in the barrel-sandwich hybrid fold (b.84), but occurs in single copy in the α/β-hammerhead fold (d.41) and in two other folds (e.29 and f.46).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and Figure 3.

claim: The β-hammerhead motif occurs in single copy in the α/β-hammerhead fold (d.41) and in two other folds (e.29 and f.46).
source: Also, the β-hammerhead motif (Figure 1B, Figure 3: 12), which resembles a hammerhead, is duplicated in the barrel-sandwich hybrid fold (b.84), but occurs in single copy in the α/β-hammerhead fold (d.41) and in two other folds (e.29 and f.46).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B and Figure 3.

claim: The outer membrane β-hairpin forms β-barrels of between four and twelve hairpins.

claim: Repetition and accretion must have been the key forces in the emergence of domains.
source: Our findings thus indicate that repetition and accretion must have been the key forces in the emergence of domains.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings about fragment occurrence.

claim: Andrew McLachlan charted out in more than 20 publications the origin of many proteins by repetition.
source: Starting in the 1970's Andrew McLachlan charted out in more than 20 publications the origin of many proteins by repetition (McLachlan, 1972; 1987), in some cases clearly of subdomain-sized fragments (Blundell et al., 1979; McLachlan, 1980; 1980).
evidence: This is a historical reference supported by citations.

claim: Analyses of fold space have shown the high incidence of repetitive folds, amounting to as many as one fifth of all folds.
source: Aided by computational tools to detect repeats in sequence (Heger and Holm, 2000; Szklarczyk and Heringa, 2004; Biegert and Soding, 2008) and structure (Kim et al., 2010; Myers-Turnbull et al., 2014), analyses of fold space have shown the high incidence of repetitive folds, amounting to as many as one fifth of all folds (Andrade et al., 2001; Balaji, 2015; Forrest, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Of the 10 most populated folds in SCOPe, 6 (including the top 5), have repetitive structures.
source: These include some of the most frequent folds, such as ferredoxins (Eck and Dayhoff, 1966), immunoglobulins (Huang and Xiao, 2007), β-propellers (Murzin, 1992) and TIM-barrels (Soding et al., 2006); indeed, of the 10 most populated folds in SCOPe, 6 (including the top 5), have repetitive structures and all of them have members in which the repetition is also detectable at the sequence level.
evidence: This is based on analysis of SCOPe data.

claim: All of the 10 most populated folds in SCOPe have members in which the repetition is also detectable at the sequence level.

source: Our fragments are spread across a total of 130 folds and 188 superfamilies in SCOPe.

source: Given that the current version of SCOPe comprises 1194 folds and 1961 superfamilies, they could be considered to cover only a small of fraction.

source: However, of the 25 most populated folds in SCOPe, which comprise about 25% of all superfamilies, 14 contain one of the fragments and 7 of the top 10 do.

claim: The fragments are widespread in today's domains.
source: We conclude that, far from being anecdotal, our fragments are indeed widespread in today's domains.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the distribution analysis.

claim: The 40 fragments described represent a lower bound.
source: The 40 fragments we describe clearly represent a lower bound, given the stringent significance cut-offs in our study, the as yet incomplete fold assignment for known structures, and the fact that some ancestral fragments may have survived only in a single fold and are thus invisible to our method.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the limitations of the study.

claim: Relaxing the sequence similarity requirement to a probability of 60% leads to the inclusion of 5 further fragments.
source: With respect to the significance cut-offs we find, for example, that relaxing the sequence similarity requirement to a probability of 60% leads to the inclusion of 5 further fragments, some with substantial arguments in their favor, such as the aforementioned ASP-box (Copley et al., 2001) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1: B1, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This describes the effect of relaxing the cutoff criteria.

claim: The number of ancestral fragments that could be reconstructed at a satisfactory level of confidence may well approach 100 in the next decades.
source: For these reasons we think that the number of ancestral fragments that could be reconstructed at a satisfactory level of confidence may well approach 100 in the next decades.
evidence: This is a speculative projection about future work.

claim: The set of 40 fragments should cover both the most frequent and best conserved ancestral peptides.
source: Nevertheless, the set of 40 fragments we have described here should cover both the most frequent and best conserved ancestral peptides, and support a viable theory for the emergence of folded proteins.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what the current set represents.

claim: The set of 40 fragments supports a viable theory for the emergence of folded proteins.
source: Nevertheless, the set of 40 fragments we have described here should cover both the most frequent and best conserved ancestral peptides, and support a viable theory for the emergence of folded proteins.
